--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.constraint()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Calculate Burt's constraint for each node. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.constraint()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Calculate Burt's constraint for each node. title: >- [Graph.constraint()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Calculate Burt's constraint for each node. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Calculate Burt's constraint for each node. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L50801-L50988){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.constraint( weight_attr=None, attr_name=None, return_dict=False, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Burt's constraint](../assets/graphs/constraint.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The shared seven-node strip of triangles with a tail, shaded by Burt's constraint. The pendant G, with a single contact, is fully constrained at 1.00, and A, whose two contacts know each other, follows at 0.84. The bridge E, linking the triangles to the tail, spans a structural hole and has the lowest constraint, 0.48." width="100%"} Burt's constraint measures the extent to which ego's contacts are redundant, that is, connected to each other. Higher constraint indicates fewer structural holes and less brokerage opportunity. Lower constraint indicates a network position with more non-redundant contacts, offering greater access to diverse information and control benefits. The constraint of node i's ego network is: `C_i = Σ_j (p_ij + Σ_q p_iq × p_qj)²` where `p_ij` are proportional tie strengths: `p_ij = (a_ij + a_ji) / Σ_k (a_ik + a_ki)` and `a_ij` are elements of the adjacency matrix (edge weights). The sums run over the node's contacts, its neighbors in either direction; on a directed graph that includes in-neighbors, so a node with only incoming edges still gets a value (NetworkX returns `nan` for it). Results otherwise match `networkx.constraint()`. Time complexity: `O(V × D²)` where `D` is average degree Space complexity: `O(V)` ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [weight_attr]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the edge attribute to use as tie strength. If `None` (default) or `"weight"`, the edge's weight field is used. Edges without a (numeric) value count as `1.0`, so on an unweighted graph all ties are equal. Parallel edges add up their weights; on a directed graph `a_ij` and `a_ji` are the arcs in each direction. [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the node attribute to store constraint values. If `None`, uses `constraint` as the attribute name. [return_dict]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, returns a dictionary mapping node IDs to constraint values. If `False`, stores values as node attributes and returns the Graph for chaining. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict[int, float | None] or Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_dict=` is `True`, a dictionary mapping node IDs to constraint values is returned. Returns `None` for isolated nodes, including nodes whose only edge is a self-loop (undefined constraint, `nan` in NetworkX). If `return_dict=` is `False`, returns self for method chaining. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} A constraint value close to $1$ says ego's contacts are tightly interlinked, so any one tie is largely redundant with the others: high closure, little room for brokerage. Values approaching $0$ mark the opposite regime: ego's contacts sit in structural holes, disconnected from one another, and information or influence flowing between them must pass through ego. Burt (1992) formalizes this as $c_i = \sum_j \left(p_{ij} + \sum_q p_{iq}\,p_{qj}\right)^2$, where $p_{ij}$ is the share of ego's tie strength invested in contact $j$; the inner sum captures indirect ties routed through mutual contacts $q$, and squaring rewards concentration. The low-constraint positions are the ones network theorists usually care about, since they concentrate the classic structural-hole payoffs: access to non-redundant information, control over what crosses between otherwise separate groups, and the ability to recombine ideas from disconnected clusters. That makes constraint a natural instrument for social-capital studies, innovation research, and any organizational analysis hunting for boundary spanners or entrepreneurial positions. Isolated nodes return `None` because there is no ego network to measure over. ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~effective_size`) : The other half of Burt's structural holes measures. [](`~local_constraint`) : The constraint that one neighbor puts on a node. [](`~betweenness_centrality`) : A path-based view of brokerage. ## Examples {.doc-examples} B has three contacts, and only two of them know each other, so B has the lowest constraint. A depends on B alone and scores `1`. C and D each have two contacts who know each other, which makes them the most constrained, slightly above `1` (the measure allows it): ::: {#d3e4f8b5 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph.from_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("B", "D"), ("C", "D")]) graph.constraint().get_node_df().select("label", "constraint") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: Each contact's share of the score is its `local_constraint()`, and `effective_size()` measures the same redundancy as a number of contacts.
